title: Headlight restoration: inspection, referral and protection
audience: Car detailers who offer headlight restoration as a service, and staff who must decide whether a lamp suits surface restoration or must be referred.
learningOutcomes: Explain why polycarbonate lenses haze and yellow, and separate a surface problem from a crack, internal fogging or a housing fault.
Inspect a headlamp and choose between surface restoration and referral, applying the referral rule in this lesson.
Mask and protect surrounding paint, trim and seals, and handle dust and wet slurry in line with the product label and SDS.
Describe to the customer what restoration can and cannot achieve, and record consent and before and after evidence.

instruction.heading: Why lenses haze and yellow
instruction.body: Most modern headlamp lenses are made from polycarbonate, a plastic chosen for toughness and light weight. The Spanish-language manual in the source set names sun exposure as the main factor in the dulling, and this lesson starts from the same point. Sunlight wears the outer face of the lens over time, and the surface loses its clarity, so light scatters instead of passing cleanly through. The cloudy, yellowish look most owners recognise is a surface condition. Restoration works on that outer layer only. It does not reverse damage that goes deeper. A crack, moisture trapped behind the lens, or a failed seal belongs to a different category, because a surface process cannot close a gap in the plastic or dry out the inside of a housing. Check the lamp or lens manufacturer's material information before you state it to a customer as fact. This lesson does not claim that restoration returns light output to factory standard. That needs a measurement and is outside this service.

instruction.heading: Inspecting the lamp and choosing restore or refer
instruction.body: Inspect every lamp before you quote. Look at it in daylight and, where it is safe to do so, at night with the lamp working, as the owner directs. Note the type of haze and where it sits on the lens. Even surface haze that feels smooth to the touch is the condition restoration is designed for. Also note any crack or chip, pitting, a peeling coat, condensation or water inside the lens, a cracked or distorted housing, broken or loose mounting points, a discoloured or melted housing, and any sign of an electrical fault such as a dim, flickering or failed lamp. Photograph each finding before any work starts. Choose restoration only when the lens is intact and sealed, the damage is on the outer face, and no trigger in the referral rule applies. Skipping this inspection creates a scope problem as well as a workmanship problem, as “Service boundaries and consent” explains.

instruction.heading: Masking and protecting paint and trim
instruction.body: Masking protects the paint, the grille, badges, bumper edges and any rubber seal around the lamp. Use a low-tack masking tape with a clean, firm edge, so it does not lift when the surface is wet. Some restoration work carries liquid and slurry across the lamp and its surroundings, so cover any area the liquid could reach that tape does not protect. Check every tape line before you start, and again after the first wet stage, because tape can loosen when it is wet. Keep tape off the lens seal where you can, since adhesive residue there makes the final seal harder to inspect. The English guides in the source set describe masking headlights and trim as routine. The tape type and how long it stays on come from the tape maker's and the product's labels, not from this lesson.

instruction.heading: Wet sanding and polishing in general terms
instruction.body: The aim is to remove the thin, damaged outer layer of plastic, then bring the surface back to a clear, smooth finish. Work on a wet surface with light, even pressure, and keep it wet throughout. Dry sanding generates heat and dust and can mark the lens. Begin with the abrasive that the restoration product or its label names for the first stage, then move through the finer stages the label lists. The specific abrasives, their order, the speed and the water-to-product mix are product-specific. This lesson does not state them, and the sequence in the Spanish manual is not adopted here. After each stage, rinse the lens and inspect it under good light for an even haze and for deeper scratches. If an area stays dull or a scratch remains, return to the previous stage rather than pressing harder. Stop and reassess if the plastic becomes warm, if the surface turns cloudy or changes texture, or if you think the lens is getting thin. Then polish with a labelled polish to bring out clarity and smoothness, and inspect again before any protection is applied.

instruction.heading: UV-protective clear coat and when it is needed
instruction.body: Once the surface is clean and clear, the lens is bare plastic and has lost any protection it had. The Spanish manual lists a protective varnish or seal as an option for longer-lasting results, and the English guides stress UV protection whenever a plastic surface is treated. Apply a UV-protective clear coat when the restoration removed the outer layer that carried protection, or when the lens has no protection left, and when the product label names polycarbonate lenses as a suitable surface. Apply it only to a clean, dry, polished lens, within the temperature and humidity range the label gives, and in the number of coats the label specifies. A protective coat is not a repair. It does not fill a crack or stop moisture getting inside the housing. Do not promise how long the protection lasts. Durability depends on the product, the surface, the conditions and how the car is used, so state only what the label supports.

instruction.heading: Cleaning and drying afterwards
instruction.body: When the last stage is complete, rinse the lens and the surrounding area with clean water, so polish and slurry do not dry on the paint or the seal. Dry the lens with clean, dry microfibre, and do not rub it into the seal. Look closely at the lens edge and the seal for water or fog inside the housing. Water inside the lens is a referral trigger, not something to dry and hand back. Remove the masking slowly, pulling back on itself at a low angle, and check the paint edges for residue. Then inspect the lamp again in the same light as the first inspection, so the before and after photographs can be compared fairly. If you can switch the lamp on safely, check that it works and looks as it did before. Do not open the housing to check the wiring. That is electrical work and sits outside this service.

instruction.heading: Dust and wet-slurry handling
instruction.body: Sanding produces dust, and the way you handle it matters for the worker and for the surroundings. Wet methods keep dust down, so keep the surface and the abrasive wet throughout. Dry sweeping, blowing with compressed air and dry buffing spread dust into the air and onto nearby surfaces, so avoid them. Slurry from sanding and polishing contains the abrasive, the product and fragments of the lens. Do not let it run into a stormwater drain. Collect it, let the solids settle or absorb the liquid, and dispose of it as the product's SDS waste section directs and as local council or water authority rules require. Clean the work area with a wet method after each job. Wash cloths and applicators used for restoration separately from other cleaning items, and keep food and drink out of the area while dust or slurry is present.

instruction.heading: PPE and respiratory protection for dust
instruction.body: Read the SDS for each product before the job, and focus on the sections for personal protection and handling, because that is where the practical instructions sit. Eye protection and gloves are usually needed for polish, slurry and abrasive products, but the SDS decides which types. For dust, the first control is to reduce it at the source, using wet methods and ventilation that moves air away from the worker. Respiratory protective equipment is the last line of control. Basic dust masks and surgical masks do not protect against small particles, so they are not a substitute for a respirator. Where a respirator is needed after other controls, use a tight-fitting type that seals to the face. Each worker needs their own fit test before first use, at least once a year, and after a significant change in facial features such as major weight change. Each person also does a fit check every time they put the respirator on. Facial hair that breaks the seal can stop a respirator sealing. Particulate filters are classed P1, P2 or P3, with P3 giving the highest protection, and the class is chosen from the hazard assessment and the SDS. Respirators used at work should comply with AS/NZS 1716.

instruction.heading: Electrical and lamp safety
instruction.body: Headlamps are electrical components, even when the work is on the lens. Restoration sits on the outside of the lens and does not include wiring, connectors, control units, ballasts or diagnosis of any fault. Only licensed or registered electricians should carry out electrical work, and this lesson does not grant any licence or authority to do it. Check leads and power tools for damage before each use, and remove any damaged lead from service. Keep leads off the floor where they can be damaged or reached by water, and use leads rated for damp conditions where the work is near water. Halogen lamps can stay hot after use, so let them cool before you touch the housing. Treat a lamp that flickers, is dim or will not light as an electrical fault. Record it and refer it. Do not attempt to make it work.

instruction.heading: Chemical hazards from the SDS
instruction.body: Each product in a restoration kit, and each cleaner or protective coat you use, has an SDS. Read its sections on hazard identification, first aid, handling and storage, exposure controls and personal protection, and disposal before the job starts. Check for skin and eye hazards, inhalation hazards, flammability and any incompatibility with other products you use. Under the WHS duties for hazardous chemicals, a business must identify and assess the risks, control them, store the chemicals safely and communicate hazard information to workers. Safe Work Australia's SDS guidance says that workers who use, handle or store a chemical should be able to reach its SDS, and that the business must make it easy to access. That page covers access, not practical handling, so the handling and PPE details come from the SDS itself. Keep products in their original labelled containers, and keep the SDS where the team can reach it, either in the vehicle or in a file at the site.

instruction.heading: What restoration can and cannot promise
instruction.body: Restoration improves the clarity of the outer surface of an intact lens. It does not repair cracks, seal a housing, remove moisture from inside a lamp, fix an electrical fault, or guarantee that the lamp will pass any inspection. Outcomes depend on the lens age and material, the damage, any earlier treatment, the product used, and how the car is kept and driven. Consumer law applies to what you say. Under the ACCC's guidance, claims about a product's benefits and performance must be provable, and leaving out relevant details can mislead a customer even without any intent to mislead. Do not say that a restored lamp will stay clear for a set time, or that it is protected for life, unless you hold evidence that supports the statement. Set out in the quote what is included, what is excluded, the condition of each lamp, and any referral items. Ask the owner to confirm the agreed scope in writing before work begins.

instruction.heading: Documentation and consent
instruction.body: Documentation protects the owner, the business and you. Before work, photograph each lamp from the front and from one side, in the same light, and record its condition, including any damage that was already there. Record the owner's consent to restoration, the agreed scope and the limits you explained. After the work, take matching photographs in matching light. Record the products used by name, the label reference, the SDS reference, the stages used in general terms, the protective coat applied and its label conditions, the drying check, and any referral. Keep photographs to the job, and keep them only as long as your business's privacy and records practice allows.

instruction.heading: Referral rule
instruction.body: Refer, rather than restore, when any of the following is present: a crack in the lens; moisture or fog inside the lens that does not clear after the lamp has dried; a cracked, broken or distorted housing; a broken or loose mounting point or seal; a melted, scorched or discoloured housing; or an electrical fault such as a dim, flickering or failed lamp. A referral means stopping work on that lamp, recording the finding with photographs, telling the owner in writing what you found and what restoration cannot fix, and passing the repair to a qualified repairer. Where the referral affects other work on the vehicle, agree the next step with the owner before you continue. A referral is part of a responsible service, not a failure of it. This lesson does not grant authority to repair a lamp, a housing or any wiring.

procedure: Confirm the job scope and the owner's consent to restoration and its limits, in writing.
Inspect each lamp in daylight and, where safe, with the lamp working. Photograph every finding before work starts.
Apply the referral rule. Refer any lamp that meets a trigger, and record it before going further.
Read the SDS for each product. Set up PPE and any respiratory protection the risk assessment requires, with a fit check for any respirator.
Mask the paint, trim and seal, then check each tape line.
Clean the lens with a wet method to remove loose grit.
Work the surface wet, following the label stages in order, and inspect the lens between stages.
Polish with the labelled polish and inspect for clarity and smoothness.
Apply a UV-protective clear coat where needed, within the label conditions.
Rinse and dry the lens, then check for water or fog inside it. Refer if any is present.
Remove the masking, check the paint edges, and inspect the lamp in the same light as the before photographs.
Photograph the after state, complete the record and the signed scope, and handle dust and slurry as described above.

workedExamples.situation: Invented example: A hatchback has two lenses with even, light haze. Both feel smooth, both are sealed, and neither has a crack or moisture inside. The owner parks outdoors.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is this a restoration job, and what must the quote contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: Yes. The damage is on the outer face and no referral trigger applies, so restoration is within scope. The quote lists the included stages, the protective coat and its conditions, and the exclusions, including cracks, moisture and electrical faults. It states that clarity cannot be guaranteed for a set period. The owner confirms the scope in writing, and the before photographs are taken first.

workedExamples.situation: Invented example: A sedan's left lens has a hairline crack near a mounting point, with fog inside that remains after the lamp has been running for a while. The owner asks for both lenses to be made clear and wants a promise that they will stay clear for five years.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What happens to the left lamp, and what do you say about the five-year request?
workedExamples.reasoning: Refer the left lamp. The crack and the internal fog are referral triggers, and surface restoration fixes neither. Record the findings with photographs and tell the owner in writing. Do not give the five-year promise, because the business cannot support it with evidence. The right lamp can go through the normal process once the owner has agreed the revised scope.

workedExamples.situation: Invented example: A restored lens is ready for protection. The customer asks whether the clear coat will stop the lens yellowing for good. The product label gives application conditions, and the owner says the car sits in full sun for most of the day.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you check before applying the coat, and what do you tell the owner?
workedExamples.reasoning: Check the label's application conditions against the day's temperature, humidity and the surface state, and apply the coat only if they are met. Tell the owner that the coat is protection, not a guarantee, and that no period of protection can be promised. Explain that full sun exposure is a factor in how the lens ages. Record the conditions checked and what the owner was told.

equipmentAndPpe: Good daylight for inspection, plus a torch for the lamp housing edge.
Low-tack masking tape with a clean edge, and film or covers for trim and seals.
Wet-method supplies: clean water, a labelled spray bottle, and a pad or sponge suited to the product label.
Abrasives and polishes named on the product label, used in the labelled order only.
A UV-protective clear coat, used only where its label supports lens use.
Microfibre cloths in labelled groups, kept clean and dry.
Camera or phone with a consistent setting for before and after photographs.
PPE as the SDS requires, including eye protection and gloves. A respirator only where the risk assessment calls for it, with a fit test and fit check record.
Leads and power tools checked for damage before each use.
Labelled waste containers for slurry and used cloths, handled as the SDS and local rules direct.

commonErrors.error: Restoring a lens that has a crack or fog inside.
commonErrors.prevention: Apply the referral rule at inspection, and refer before any work starts.

commonErrors.error: Sanding dry, or pressing harder to speed up the job.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep the surface wet, use light pressure, and go back a stage if an area stays dull.

commonErrors.error: Promising that a restored lens will stay clear for a set period.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe limits in the quote, and state only durability the label supports.

commonErrors.error: Using a basic dust mask as respiratory protection for sanding dust.
commonErrors.prevention: Use local controls first. If a respirator is needed, use a tight-fitting type with a fit test and a fit check.

commonErrors.error: Letting slurry run into a drain or onto the ground.
commonErrors.prevention: Collect the slurry and dispose of it as the SDS and local rules direct.

commonErrors.error: Opening the housing to fix a flicker.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the electrical fault and refer it to a qualified repairer.

commonErrors.error: Applying the protective coat to a damp or unfinished lens.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the surface is clean and dry, and within the label's application conditions, before coating.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Under the WHS duties for hazardous chemicals, a business must identify and assess the risks, control them, store the chemicals safely and communicate hazard information to workers. Source: Safe Work Australia, WHS duties related to hazardous chemicals (checked 2026-11-03; no page date shown).

Workers who use, handle or store a chemical should be able to reach its SDS, and the business must make it easy to access. The SDS handling and PPE sections give the practical controls. Source: Safe Work Australia, Using safety data sheets (checked 2026-11-03; no page date shown).

Respiratory protective equipment is a last-line control, considered after local controls such as ventilation. Basic and surgical dust masks do not protect against small particles. Tight-fitting respirators need a fit test before first use, at least yearly, and a fit check each time they are worn. Respirators used at work should comply with AS/NZS 1716. Source: WorkSafe Queensland, Respiratory protective equipment (RPE) (checked 2026-11-03; no page date shown). Queensland is an example. The regulator for your state or territory sets the rules that apply to you.

Only licensed or registered electricians should carry out electrical work. Lamp wiring, connectors, control units and ballasts are outside this service, and this lesson does not grant any licence or authority for that work. Source: Safe Work Australia, Electrical safety: managing risks (checked 2026-11-03; no page date shown).
Check leads and power tools for damage before each use, and remove damaged leads from service. Source: Safe Work Australia, Electrical safety: managing risks (checked 2026-11-03; no page date shown).

Claims about a product's benefits and performance must be provable, and leaving out relevant details can be misleading. Source: ACCC, False or misleading claims (page dated 28 June 2026; checked 2026-11-03).
Check them with your council, water authority, state or territory regulator, or a qualified adviser.

This lesson covers surface restoration only. It does not grant any licence, certificate or authority for electrical, glazing, body or vehicle repair work, and completing it does not qualify a person for that work.

qualityStandard: Each lamp is inspected, and the restore or refer decision is recorded, before any work starts.
No restoration is carried out on a lamp that meets a referral trigger.
Surrounding paint, trim and seals are masked, and no product mark is left on them at handover.
The protective coat is applied only within the label conditions, and no durability is promised beyond what the label supports.
The lamp is dry inside, the before and after photographs match in light and angle, and the owner has confirmed the scope.
documentationEvidence: Before and after photographs of each lamp, in matching light and from matching angles.
Owner consent and confirmed scope, including the limits explained to the owner.
Product, label and SDS references, the stages used in general terms, and the protective coat conditions.
Referral record for any lamp that met a trigger, with photographs and written notice to the owner.
PPE and fit-check record, where a respirator was used.
summary: Restoration works on the outer face of an intact lens. A crack, internal fog, a damaged housing or an electrical fault is a referral.
Mask, work wet, follow the label stages in order, and inspect between stages.
Apply protection only as the label supports, and state only what you can prove.
Handle dust and slurry by wet methods and the SDS, and document every step.

knowledgeChecks.question: A headlamp lens has a fine crack, and moisture is visible inside it. What is the correct action?
options: Polish the outside to hide the crack and hand the car back, since the crack will not be seen once the lens is bright and shiny for the owner
Record the findings with photographs, refer the lamp to a qualified repairer, and tell the owner in writing that surface restoration does not fix the crack
Seal the crack with a clear coat and promise that it is watertight, so the owner has no reason to worry about any moisture in the lamp housing
Sand deeper until the crack is no longer visible, then polish the lens to a clear finish for the owner to inspect at pickup time and sign off on the job

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must a restorer avoid promising that a restored lens will stay clear for a set period?
options: Because a claim about performance must be provable, and a claim with no evidence behind it can mislead under ACCC guidance
Because the owner can always claim that the clarity period is unlimited, so no limit needs to be stated at all
Because clear coat is never needed on a restored lens, so any period can be stated freely to the owner today
Because a restorer is not allowed to discuss the condition of a lamp with the owner before the job starts at all

knowledgeChecks.question: A restorer is sanding a lens and the dust is building up. Which control comes first?
options: Put on a basic dust mask and carry on with the sanding, since that is enough for most small jobs in the workshop and the dust is not a concern for the owner
Use a tight-fitting respirator without any other step, since it protects the worker fully from every type of dust in the workshop at all times
Use local controls such as wet methods and ventilation first, and use a respirator only if the risk assessment still requires one, with a fit test and a fit check
Blow the dust off with compressed air so the lens is easier to see, then keep sanding until the surface is clear, bright and ready for the owner to inspect

knowledgeChecks.question: After restoration, a headlamp flickers and is dim. What is the correct action?
options: Open the housing and rewire the lamp yourself, since a quick fix at the workshop bench will solve the flicker and dimming and the owner will be pleased with the fast result
Stop, photograph and record the fault, and refer the electrical work to a licensed or registered electrician or qualified repairer, since this lesson does not cover it
Tape the wire and hand back the car, since the tape will hold the connection safely until the owner gets it looked at by a service centre in the following weeks
Spray a contact cleaner onto the lamp connector and check again, since a clean connection usually fixes the flicker and the dimming straight away
